title: Hart's union of rules
subtitle: Primary and secondary rules, the rule of recognition, and the limits of language
objectives: Explain Hart's central claim that law is best understood as a union of primary and secondary rules, and state how this reframing answers the three objections to Austin's command theory
State the three secondary rules — recognition, change, adjudication — and the specific defect of a purely primary-rule system each one cures
Explain the internal/external point of view distinction and the 'open texture' of language, including why judges exercise genuine discretion in penumbral cases

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hart, The Concept of Law (1961), chs 2–7
leadingAuthorities.role: The central text: primary/secondary rules, the rule of recognition, internal/external point of view, open texture

leadingAuthorities.citation: Austin, The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832)
leadingAuthorities.role: The command theory Hart is directly answering — see Lesson 4

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Hart's Concept of Law is the single most cited text in this module and the framework most other theories in this module define themselves against. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can name the rule of recognition — this lesson checks whether you can explain what work it's actually doing.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on stating Hart's terms before. The test pool below leans towards scenarios: expect 'is this a core or penumbral case' rather than 'define open texture'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can restate Austin's three problems from Lesson 4 first — this whole lesson is built as Hart's answer to them, and the sequence won't make sense out of order.

overview.hook: H. L. A. Hart opens The Concept of Law by admitting something unusual for a legal textbook: after millennia of jurisprudence, 'What is law?' still doesn't have an agreed answer, and much of the disagreement is really disagreement about what kind of question it is. Rather than defining law as a thing, Hart reframes it as a structure — a union of two different kinds of rule, working together, that turns a society's diffuse social pressure into a functioning legal system. This lesson is that structure, and the two ideas — the internal point of view, and the open texture of language — that make it do real explanatory work.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson teaches a fixed historical text (1961) and the settled scholarly reading of it. Law stated as at 23 September 2026 reflects only that this content remains current teaching.

parts.heading: Hart's diagnosis: what Austin's model left out
parts.voice: argumentative — recaps the failure before offering the fix
body: Lesson 4 left three problems on the table: a command theory struggles to explain how law can continue in force without being re-issued by each new sovereign, struggles to explain power-conferring rules that don't order anyone to do anything, and struggles to identify a sovereign who is itself unconstrained by any prior rule in a modern constitutional state.

Hart's diagnosis is that all three problems share a single root cause: Austin tried to build an entire legal system out of one kind of rule — rules that impose duties, backed by threats, the way the gunman's threat does. Hart calls these primary rules, and he doesn't deny they're a real and necessary part of law. His claim is that primary rules alone can never add up to a legal system, however many of them you pile up, however habitually they're obeyed.

What's missing, on Hart's account, are rules about rules — a second layer that lets a society identify which primary rules count as law, change them deliberately, and resolve disputes about whether they've been broken. Law, for Hart, is 'the union of primary and secondary rules' — and that union, not the sovereign's threat, is what a mature legal system actually is.

components.definition: Rules that impose duties — requiring or forbidding certain conduct, such as the criminal law's prohibition on theft or violence. A society could, in principle, have only primary rules, resting on diffuse social pressure rather than a legal system in Hart's full sense.

interaction.prompt: According to Hart, what is the single root cause of Austin's three problems (continuing law, power-conferring rules, the illimitable sovereign)?
options: Austin tried to build an entire legal system out of primary, duty-imposing rules alone, with no second layer of rules about rules
Austin didn't believe sanctions were necessary for law at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Hart's move is structural: he doesn't reject sanctions or duty-imposing rules, he argues they're only half of what a legal system needs — and that missing half is a distinct kind of rule, not just more of the same kind.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — Austin's problem for Hart isn't that he over- or under-used sanctions, it's that his whole model is built from one kind of rule (primary, duty-imposing rules) with no second layer of rules about rules to identify, change or adjudicate them.

parts.heading: Life with only primary rules: three defects
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Imagine a simple society governed entirely by primary rules of obligation, maintained only by diffuse social pressure — no legislature, no courts, no officials. Hart argues such a regime, even if fairly stable, would suffer three specific defects, and each defect points directly at the secondary rule needed to cure it.

Uncertainty: with no way to identify which social rules are actually binding obligations, disputes about the rules themselves — does this rule exist, does it apply here — have no agreed way to be settled. Static character: the only way such rules change is slow, informal social evolution; there's no deliberate mechanism for a society to create new rules or abolish old ones as circumstances change. Inefficiency: disputes about whether a rule has been broken, and what should be done about it, are settled (if at all) by the diffuse and unfocused pressure of public opinion, with no authoritative body to decide.

components.label: The three defects of a pre-legal, primary-rules-only regime
points: Uncertainty — no way to identify definitively which rules are binding
Static character — no deliberate mechanism to create, amend or repeal rules
Inefficiency — no authoritative body to determine breaches and enforce outcomes; only diffuse social pressure

interaction.prompt: Match the reasoning: put these steps in the order Hart's argument runs.
items: A society has only primary, duty-imposing rules maintained by social pressure
Hart identifies three structural defects this regime necessarily suffers
Each defect corresponds to the absence of a specific kind of secondary rule
Introducing all three secondary rules turns a pre-legal regime into a legal system
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the whole architecture of Hart's argument: diagnose the defects of a primary-rules-only world first, then show each secondary rule exists precisely to cure one of them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — Hart starts from the pre-legal regime, identifies its three defects, then shows each secondary rule is the specific cure for one defect, and only the combination produces a full legal system.

parts.heading: Secondary rules: the remedy for each defect
parts.voice: structural — maps cure to defect directly
body: Each secondary rule Hart introduces answers exactly one of the three defects, and the pairing is worth learning precisely, because exam questions routinely test whether you can match cure to defect rather than just list all four terms.

The rule of recognition cures uncertainty: it supplies the criteria by which a society's officials — paradigmatically, its courts — identify which rules count as valid law. In the UK, something like 'what the Queen (or King) in Parliament enacts is law' functions this way. The rule of change cures the static character of the pre-legal world: it confers power on someone (a legislature) to introduce new primary rules and repeal old ones deliberately, rather than waiting on slow social evolution. The rule of adjudication cures inefficiency: it confers power on someone (courts) to determine, authoritatively, whether a primary rule has been broken on a given occasion, replacing diffuse social pressure with a decision that settles the dispute.

Of the three, the rule of recognition does the most theoretical work, because it is also Hart's answer to the question command theory couldn't answer: what ultimately makes a rule law at all. It replaces Austin's sovereign — a person — with a social rule practised by officials.

components.title: Defect to cure
components.description: Mapping each defect of a primary-rules-only regime to the secondary rule that cures it.

nodes.label: Defect: uncertainty about which rules are binding
Cure: rule of recognition — supplies criteria of validity
Defect: static character, no deliberate mechanism to change rules
Cure: rule of change — confers power to create/repeal rules
Defect: inefficiency of diffuse social pressure in resolving disputes
Cure: rule of adjudication — confers power to determine breaches authoritatively

components.textAlternative: Uncertainty about which rules bind is cured by the rule of recognition, which supplies criteria of validity. Static character — no deliberate way to change rules — is cured by the rule of change, which confers a power to create and repeal rules. Inefficiency in resolving disputes is cured by the rule of adjudication, which confers a power to determine breaches authoritatively.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario illustrates the rule of change, rather than the rule of adjudication?
interaction.scenarioA: A court is asked to decide whether a particular defendant's conduct breached an existing statutory rule, and issues a binding ruling settling the dispute.
interaction.scenarioB: A legislature votes to repeal an outdated statute and enact a new one addressing the same subject matter differently.
interaction.explanation: B is the rule of change in action: a deliberate, rule-governed mechanism for creating and repealing primary rules, curing the static character of a pre-legal regime. A is the rule of adjudication: settling, authoritatively, whether an existing rule has been broken.

parts.heading: The rule of recognition and the internal point of view
parts.voice: conceptual — introduces the distinction that separates Hart from a purely external, predictive account of law
body: The rule of recognition is not itself validated by some further rule — it is, Hart says, simply accepted and practised as a common standard by a legal system's officials, most importantly its courts. Its existence is a social fact: you establish what it is by observing what criteria of validity officials actually use, not by looking for a rule that authorises it.

This is where Hart's second key move comes in: the distinction between the internal and the external point of view. An external observer — a sociologist, an anthropologist, a hostile foreign power — can describe a legal system purely predictively: 'when officials do X, courts tend to respond with Y.' That's a legitimate description, but it misses something a participant inside the system experiences: officials (and most citizens) don't just predict that a rule will be enforced, they accept it as a standard of correct behaviour, use it to criticise deviations, and feel it justifies their own and others' conduct.

Hart's claim is that you cannot fully explain law from the external point of view alone — a predictive account, of the kind American legal realism offers, misses the normative, rule-following character that officials themselves experience from the inside. A theory of law has to capture both perspectives to be complete.

components.citation: Hart, The Concept of Law, ch. 5
components.text: What is necessary is that there should be a critical reflective attitude to certain patterns of behaviour as a common standard, and that this should display itself in criticism (including self-criticism), demands for conformity, and in acknowledgements that such criticism and demands are justified.
elements: The internal point of view is a critical, reflective acceptance of a rule as a standard, not mere predicted compliance
It shows itself in criticism of deviation, demands for conformity, and acknowledgment that such demands are justified
The external point of view merely predicts patterns of behaviour without this normative attitude

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Hart's 'internal point of view' simply means predicting, with high confidence, that officials will enforce a rule?
sliderLabels: Confident — that is not what it means
interaction.correctPosition: that is not what it means
interaction.explanation: That is not Hart's claim. Prediction is the external point of view — an observer noting a pattern. The internal point of view is a distinct, normative attitude: officials accepting the rule as a standard of correct conduct, criticising deviations from it, and treating that criticism as justified. It's the difference between describing a rule and using one.

parts.heading: Open texture: why rules run out
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds through Hart's own famous example
body: Hart's second lasting contribution addresses a different problem: even once you know which rules are valid law, ordinary language doesn't always tell you, with certainty, whether a given rule applies to a given case. Hart illustrates this with a rule he invented for the purpose: 'no vehicles in the park.'

A car is obviously a vehicle — a core, settled instance the rule plainly covers. But what about a bicycle? A child's electric scooter? A wartime tank mounted on a plinth as a war memorial? Hart calls this the open texture of language: general terms have a core of settled meaning surrounded by a penumbra of genuine uncertainty, where competent speakers of the language could reasonably disagree.

This matters enormously for adjudication. In the core, a judge is simply applying a settled rule. In the penumbra, Hart argues, a judge is doing something closer to legislating in miniature — exercising a real, bounded discretion to decide what the rule should mean here, guided by its evident purpose, but not simply 'discovering' a pre-existing answer. This is a genuinely contested claim, not a settled one: Hart's critics — Dworkin most prominently, in a later lesson in this module — will argue there is far less true discretion, and far more law to work with even at the edges, than Hart allows.

components.definition: Hart's term for the inherent indeterminacy of general language: a rule has a core of settled application and a penumbra of genuinely uncertain cases, where the rule's own words don't dictate a single correct answer.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that most precisely explains why penumbral cases require judicial discretion, on Hart's account.
interaction.passage: If a penumbra of uncertainty must surround all legal rules, then their application to specific cases in the penumbral area cannot be a matter of logical deduction, and so deductive reasoning cannot serve as a model for what judges, or indeed anyone, should do in bringing particular cases under general rules. In this area men cannot live by deduction alone, and it is at their peril that they neglect the further reasoning which lies behind the maxim.
interaction.ratioSentence: If a penumbra of uncertainty must surround all legal rules, then their application to specific cases in the penumbral area cannot be a matter of logical deduction, and so deductive reasoning cannot serve as a model for what judges, or indeed anyone, should do in bringing particular cases under general rules.

testPool.prompt: State, in one sentence, Hart's central claim about what a legal system fundamentally is.
acceptableAnswers: a union of primary and secondary rules
law is the union of primary, duty-imposing rules and secondary, power-conferring rules about those rules
testPool.modelAnswer: A legal system, for Hart, is best understood as a union of primary rules (which impose duties) and secondary rules (which confer powers to identify, change and adjudicate those primary rules).

acceptableAnswers: rule of recognition, rule of change, rule of adjudication
testPool.modelAnswer: The rule of recognition, the rule of change, and the rule of adjudication.

testPool.prompt: Which secondary rule supplies the criteria by which officials identify which rules count as valid law?
options: The rule of recognition
The rule of change

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three defects Hart attributes to a purely primary-rules regime?
options: Uncertainty about which rules are binding
Static character, with no deliberate way to change rules
Excessive severity of criminal sanctions
Inefficiency of diffuse social pressure in resolving disputes
testPool.trapExplanation: Hart's three defects are structural, not about how harsh sanctions are — sanction severity plays no role in his argument at all. The defects are uncertainty, static character, and inefficiency, each cured by a distinct secondary rule.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'The rule of recognition must itself be legally valid, so there must be a further rule that validates it.' What is the strongest response to this claim?
options: The student is correct — Hart's system requires an infinite chain of validating rules
The rule of recognition is not itself valid or invalid; its existence is a social fact, constituted by its being accepted and practised by officials, particularly courts, as a common standard
Hart never addressed this question and left it as an open problem
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting error is to treat the rule of recognition as just another rule in the validity chain, needing its own further validation. Hart is explicit that this would produce an infinite regress — his point is precisely that the rule of recognition sits outside the validity chain: it is not valid, it simply exists as an accepted social practice among officials.

testPool.prompt: Put these in the correct order of Hart's argument for why an external, purely predictive account of law is incomplete.
items: An external observer can describe patterns of official behaviour predictively
This description omits how officials themselves experience following the rule
Officials display a critical, reflective attitude: criticising deviation, demanding conformity
A complete theory of law must capture this internal point of view, not prediction alone

testPool.prompt: Hart's rule 'no vehicles in the park' is chosen deliberately to illustrate open texture. Which feature of the rule does the bicycle example test?
options: Whether the term 'vehicle' has a clear core (a car) and a genuinely uncertain penumbra (a bicycle) where competent speakers could reasonably disagree
Whether parks are capable of being owned as property
Whether the rule was validly enacted under the rule of recognition

testPool.prompt: A rule reads: 'No dogs permitted in the café.' A customer brings in a small, well-behaved therapy pig on a lead. Applying Hart's open texture analysis, how should this case be classified?
options: Penumbral — a pig is plainly not the core instance ('dog') the rule was written for, but the rule's evident purpose (keeping animals out of a food environment) may or may not extend to it, leaving genuine room for reasoned disagreement
Core — any animal on a lead is automatically covered by the word 'dogs'
The rule cannot apply to this case at all, since a pig is definitionally excluded from every possible reading
testPool.explanation: This is a penumbral case in Hart's sense: the word 'dogs' plainly doesn't include 'pig' in its core meaning, but the rule's evident purpose might. Deciding it requires the kind of purposive reasoning Hart says judges genuinely exercise at the edges of a rule's application.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that illustrates the internal, rather than the external, point of view.
testPool.scenarioText: A visiting foreign journalist notes, in an article, that UK drivers reliably stop at red lights, and predicts this pattern will continue. A UK driver who runs a red light is met with sharp criticism from a passenger, who insists the driver was in the wrong and owed other road users better conduct.
tappableSpans: notes, in an article, that UK drivers reliably stop at red lights
is met with sharp criticism from a passenger
insists the driver was in the wrong
testPool.correctSpan: insists the driver was in the wrong
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the internal point of view: the passenger isn't merely predicting behaviour, they're treating the rule as a standard that justifies criticism of deviation from it — exactly the critical, reflective attitude Hart says an external, predictive account misses.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment someone treats the rule as a justified standard for criticising conduct, not merely predicting what will happen. The passenger's insistence that the driver was 'in the wrong' is the internal point of view in action; the journalist's forecast is purely external.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows a genuine rule-of-change mechanism at work, rather than the diffuse social evolution of a pre-legal regime.
testPool.scenarioText: Public attitudes towards a certain kind of conduct shift slowly over several decades, with no formal vote or enactment. Separately, a legislature holds a formal debate and votes to pass a new statute explicitly repealing an old one on the same subject.
tappableSpans: Public attitudes towards a certain kind of conduct shift slowly
a legislature holds a formal debate
votes to pass a new statute explicitly repealing an old one
testPool.correctSpan: votes to pass a new statute explicitly repealing an old one
testPool.explanation: A deliberate, rule-governed enactment and repeal is the rule of change in operation. Gradual, informal shifts in public attitude are exactly the static, unplanned kind of evolution the rule of change is designed to replace.

testPool.prompt: Which case is core, rather than penumbral, under a rule banning 'vehicles' from a public park?
testPool.scenarioA: A visitor drives an ordinary petrol car onto the park's main path to unload equipment.
testPool.scenarioB: A visitor brings in a child's ride-on toy car, battery-powered and barely faster than walking pace.
testPool.explanation: A is squarely within the rule's core meaning of 'vehicle' — an ordinary car is exactly the paradigm case the rule was written for. B sits in the penumbra: a toy car raises a genuine question about whether the rule's purpose (safety, noise, damage to the park) is engaged, on which reasonable people could differ.

testPool.prompt: A society has detailed customary rules of obligation, widely followed, but no courts and no procedure for anyone to change the rules deliberately. Applying Hart's framework, what does this society lack that prevents it from being a full legal system?
options: Secondary rules — specifically a rule of change (to alter the rules) and a rule of adjudication (to resolve disputes about them) — even though it has primary rules
Nothing — widely followed customary rules are, on Hart's account, already a complete legal system
A sovereign who is habitually obeyed by the bulk of the population
testPool.explanation: This is precisely Hart's pre-legal regime: primary rules of obligation exist and are followed, but without a rule of change or a rule of adjudication (and, implicitly, a rule of recognition to identify them with certainty), the society remains static and inefficient — it has rules, but not yet a legal system in Hart's full sense.

testPool.prompt: A local bylaw bans 'sleeping in the park overnight'. A rough sleeper argues she was not 'sleeping' but simply 'resting with her eyes closed for several hours between 1am and 5am', and that the bylaw should not apply to her. Using Hart's account of open texture and the internal/external distinction, analyse how a court should approach this dispute.
factsToOrder: The bylaw's core meaning plainly covers overnight sleeping in the park
The rough sleeper's argument tries to redescribe her conduct to escape the rule's plain language
Hart holds that penumbral cases require judges to reason from the rule's evident purpose, not deductive logic alone
Officials applying the bylaw do so from the internal point of view, treating it as a justified standard, not merely predicting enforcement

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the rough sleeper's conduct falls within the core or the penumbra of the bylaw's prohibition on 'sleeping in the park overnight', and how a court should reason about that question.
modelAnswer.rule: On Hart's account, general terms have a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of genuine uncertainty (open texture); penumbral cases cannot be resolved by deduction alone and require reasoning from the rule's evident purpose; officials apply such rules from the internal point of view, as justified standards, not as mere predictions.
modelAnswer.application: Several hours of eyes-closed rest at night, in the location and manner the bylaw is plainly aimed at, sits very close to the rule's core rather than its penumbra — the rough sleeper's redescription is an attempt to exploit language rather than a genuine case of linguistic uncertainty. Even if a court treated this as a borderline case, Hart's framework directs it to ask what purpose the bylaw serves (managing overnight occupation of the park) rather than searching for a logically compelled answer in the word 'sleeping' alone.
modelAnswer.conclusion: This is most plausibly a core case, or at most a weak penumbral one; a court applying Hart's approach would likely hold the bylaw applies, reasoning from its evident purpose rather than accepting the redescription as taking the conduct outside the rule.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that, for Hart, a judge deciding a genuinely penumbral case is simply discovering a single, pre-existing correct answer that the rule's words already contained?
sliderLabels: Confident — Hart thinks the judge is exercising a bounded discretion, not just discovering an answer
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — Hart thinks the judge is exercising a bounded discretion, not just discovering an answer
testPool.explanation: This is Hart's own, contested position: in the penumbra, the rule's language runs out, and the judge exercises a real, if bounded and purpose-guided, discretion — closer to legislating in miniature than to applying a rule that already dictated the outcome. It is exactly this claim that Dworkin will later attack, in a lesson further on in this module.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing the internal point of view into a strong prediction that a rule will be enforced. They are different claims: prediction is external and purely descriptive, while the internal point of view is normative — officials treating the rule as a standard that justifies criticism of deviation from it.
